This telescope is a cubic kilometre of ice.
It was built to catch the most elusive particle we know. The neutrino.
Nearly one hundred trillion of them pass through your body every second. You feel nothing.
They almost never touch anything. To catch even a few, you need a detector that is enormous, and crystal clear.
So at the South Pole, physicists melted eighty-six holes into the ice, with hot water.
Each hole reaches almost two and a half kilometres down.
Into them went five thousand, one hundred and sixty light sensors. Then the ice froze solid around them.
And once in a while, a neutrino hits the ice, and sets off a faint flash of light in the dark.
In twenty thirteen, after two years of watching: twenty-eight neutrinos. The first evidence of visitors from beyond our solar system.
In twenty twenty-six, that discovery earned Francis Halzen the Nobel Prize in Physics. A telescope made of ice had opened a new window on the universe.
